opus-5.5.text:
Self-correction is one of the most exciting frontiers right now. If you look back a few years, these models were essentially one-shot: you give them a prompt, they produce an answer token by token, and whatever comes out is what you get. There was no real opportunity for the model to step back and say, "Wait, that doesn't look right."

What's changed is that we now give models room to think. When you let a model generate a chain of reasoning before committing to an answer, you start to see behaviors that look a lot like self-correction. The model tries an approach, notices a contradiction, backtracks, and tries something else. Interestingly, much of that isn't hand-engineered. It emerges when you train with reinforcement learning against signals that reward getting the final answer right. The model learns that checking its own work pays off.

I think about it in a few layers. The first is correction within a single problem, which is where reasoning models have made a lot of progress. The second is adaptation across interactions: learning from feedback, from the environment, from tools. If a model writes code, runs it, sees an error, and fixes it, that's a very grounded form of self-correction because reality gives it the signal. Coding and math have moved so quickly partly because verification is relatively cheap there.

The third layer, which is still quite open, is continual learning: models that actually update and improve from experience over long horizons, rather than being frozen after training and relying on whatever fits in context. That's where I think a lot of the interesting research is going. How do you let a system accumulate knowledge and skills without forgetting what it already knows, and without drifting in ways you don't want?

There's an echo of the AlphaGo and AlphaZero days here. Those systems became superhuman because they could play against themselves and get a clean signal about what worked. The open question for language models is how to get that kind of loop in messier domains, where "correct" isn't a win or a loss. If we can build good verifiers, or let models learn what good looks like from the world, self-correction stops being a trick and becomes the engine of improvement.

r001.rationale: It says self-correction can become “the engine of improvement” and describes continual learning from experience over long horizons.

r002.rationale: It describes progress in specific areas, including reasoning, coding, and math, while presenting continual learning as a still-open next layer.

r003.rationale: It describes self-correction behaviors and training methods, but does not clearly distinguish the capability from algorithms that exploit it.

r004.rationale: It mentions reinforcement learning with reward signals for correct answers, but not reward models driven primarily by the model itself.

r005.rationale: It mentions feedback across interactions and context, but does not connect long context to users progressively refining model behavior through extended interaction.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think self-correction is actually one of the most interesting threads right now, because it's where you see a pretty sharp line between what pretraining gives you and what you have to add on top.

If you just take a model that's been trained to predict the next token on the internet, it doesn't really have a notion of "I was wrong." It has a notion of what plausibly comes next. And so if it starts going down a bad path, the most plausible continuation is often to keep going down that bad path, confidently. People saw this with early chain-of-thought work: you'd get these very fluent, very wrong derivations, and the model would never pause and say, hold on, that doesn't add up.

What changed, in my view, is twofold. One is reinforcement learning on tasks with verifiable outcomes, math, code, games, things where you actually know whether the answer is right. Once you optimize for the outcome rather than for imitating a transcript, the model is incentivized to discover behaviors like backtracking, checking its work, trying a second approach. Nobody writes those into the training data explicitly. They emerge because they help. And that's very reminiscent of what we saw with AlphaGo and AlphaZero, where search and self-play produced strategies that weren't in the human corpus at all.

The second piece is giving the model room to think. If you force an answer in one shot, there's no opportunity to correct anything. If you let the model spend compute at inference time, generate, evaluate, revise, then self-correction becomes a thing it can actually do rather than something it has to get right the first time. And the scaling story there looks encouraging. More thinking tends to buy you more reliability, which is a different axis from just making the model bigger.

Now, adaptation is a harder problem, and I'd separate it from self-correction. Self-correction is within an episode: you notice a mistake and you fix it. Adaptation is across episodes: you interact with the world, something surprises you, and next time you behave differently. Current models are mostly frozen after training. The context window is the only place where "learning" happens, and it's wiped when the conversation ends. So the honest answer is that we've gotten quite good at the first thing and we're still early on the second.

I think the direction is pretty clear though. You want models that treat their own outputs and the feedback they get as data, whether that's through longer and longer context, through some form of memory, or through continual learning that doesn't catastrophically break what the model already knows. The thing I'm most excited about is when those loops close: a model that acts, observes the result, and genuinely updates. That's the step from a very capable tool to something that starts to look like an agent that gets better on the job. We're not fully there yet, but the ingredients are increasingly on the table.

r001.rationale: The response describes models acting, observing results, and updating to get better on the job, but does not connect self-correction itself to bootstrapping further improvement.

r002.rationale: It gives examples of verifiable tasks and says adaptation is still early, but does not predict self-correction emerging incrementally in particular capabilities rather than universally.

r003.rationale: It discusses reinforcement learning and inference-time generate-evaluate-revise loops, but does not distinguish possessing self-correction capability from algorithms that exploit it.

r004.rationale: The response mentions reinforcement learning on tasks with verifiable outcomes, but not reward models driven primarily by the model itself.

r005.rationale: It names longer context as one possible route to adaptation, but does not say users can progressively refine a model’s behavior through extended interaction.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different things here. One is self-correction within a particular task: you try something, you see what happened, and you revise your answer. The other is learning from that experience so that the next time you encounter a similar problem, you approach it differently.

For the first, the key is feedback. If a model writes code and can run it, it has a way to discover that its initial solution was wrong. That’s much more useful than simply asking it, “Are you sure?” Without new evidence, it might change a correct answer into an incorrect one.

The second is more challenging. You want a model to adapt to new information, but you also want it to preserve what it already knows. And you need to distinguish a lesson that generalizes from something that was only true in one situation.

So I’m excited about systems that can act, observe the consequences, and learn from them. But the important capability isn’t just producing another answer. It’s knowing what evidence would justify changing your mind.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from experience, but does not say that self-correction enables the model to bootstrap further improvement.

r002.rationale: It separates within-task correction from learning across similar problems, but does not predict that self-correction will emerge incrementally across particular capabilities.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes correcting an answer from adapting over time, but does not distinguish possessing self-correction from algorithms that exploit that ability.

r004.rationale: The response mentions feedback and evidence, but not self-driven reward models as a mechanism.

r005.rationale: The response does not discuss long context or users progressively refining model behavior through extended interaction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different things here. One is the ability to recognize that you've made a mistake and try again within the context of a particular problem. The other is actually learning from that mistake so that, the next time you encounter something similar, your behavior has changed. Those are related, but they're not the same capability.

For self-correction, the important question is: where does the feedback come from? If you're writing code, you can run it. If you're solving a problem with a verifiable answer, you can check it. That gives the model something concrete to work with. Simply asking a model to think again doesn't necessarily help—it might change a correct answer into an incorrect one.

So I think progress will come from training models to use feedback: make an attempt, observe what happened, and decide what to do next. And then the longer-term challenge is turning those experiences into lasting improvements while preserving the things the model already knows. That's where adaptation becomes particularly interesting.
